---
title: "F2 · The numbers"
description: "Tokens, latency, throughput, memory and money: the arithmetic every chapter uses, and the constants worth memorising."
---

Most GenAI design arguments are settled by arithmetic you can do on a napkin. This chapter collects
the formulas and the constants. Every system chapter uses them, and redoing their sums with your
own inputs is the fastest way to adapt a design to your situation.

## Tokens

A token is the unit models read, write and bill. It is not a word and not a character.

| Content | Rule of thumb | Why |
|---|---|---|
| English prose | 1 token is about 0.75 words, so 1,000 tokens is about 750 words | Common words are single tokens, rare ones split |
| A dense A4 page | 500 to 700 tokens | About 400 to 500 words |
| Source code | 1 token per 3 to 4 characters | Symbols and indentation tokenise poorly |
| JSON | 20% to 40% more than the same data as CSV | Keys repeat on every row, braces and quotes cost tokens |
| Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and other Indic scripts | Often 2 to 4 times the tokens of the same content in English | Tokenisers are trained mostly on English and split these scripts into short pieces |
| An image (Claude) | About width x height / 750 tokens, so about 1,600 for a 1092 x 1092 image | Images are cut into patches; each patch costs tokens |

The Indic row matters more than any other in this table if you build for Indian users. A support
bot answering in Hindi can cost two to four times what the English version costs, with no change
in design. Tokenisers differ between vendors and generations, so measure: every major API has a
token-counting endpoint. Never compare vendors on price per token alone; compare them on price per
task, using the same inputs.

## Cost per request

$$
\text{cost} = \frac{T_{in} \cdot p_{in} + T_{out} \cdot p_{out} + T_{cached} \cdot p_{read}}{10^6}
$$

where $T$ are token counts and $p$ are prices per million tokens. Output tokens cost four to eight
times as much as input tokens on current APIs, and exactly five times on the current Claude and
GPT models. This one ratio drives a lot of design: a
system that reads 2,000 tokens and writes 400 spends as much on the 400 as on the 2,000.

::: {.numbers}
A request with 2,000 input and 400 output tokens on Claude Sonnet 5.5
  input:  2,000 x {{< var f.sonnet.in >}} / 1M = {{< var f.f2.req_in >}}
  output:   400 x {{< var f.sonnet.out >}} / 1M = {{< var f.f2.req_out >}}
  total:  {{< var f.f2.req_total >}} per request, {{< var f.f2.req_month >}} per million requests
  output share of the bill: {{< var f.f2.out_share >}}
:::

Two things make this formula lie if you are not careful. Reasoning models think before they
answer, and thinking tokens are billed as output, so a 400-token answer can cost 2,000 output tokens.
And in a multi-turn conversation or an agent loop, every turn re-sends the whole history as
input, so input tokens grow with the square of the number of turns (see
<span class="ocode">O3</span> in [F5](f5-optimisation.qmd)).

The gap between tiers is large. Claude Fable 5.1 costs {{< var f.fable.in >}} per million input
tokens; Claude Haiku 5.5 costs {{< var f.haiku.in >}}. That is a factor of
{{< var f.ratio.frontier_small >}}. Choosing the tier is the largest cost decision in most
systems, which is why [F3](f3-models.qmd) gives it a whole chapter.

## Latency

For a hosted model, one call takes:

$$
t = t_{\text{queue}} + t_{\text{prefill}} + \frac{T_{out}}{\text{decode speed}}
$$

Time to first token (queue plus prefill) is typically 300 ms to 1.5 s for hosted APIs, longer for
very long prompts and for reasoning models that think first. Decode speed is typically 40 to 150
tokens per second per stream. So output length dominates: 300 output tokens at 80 tokens per second
is 3.75 seconds, whatever you do about the network.

Three consequences show up in every chapter:

1. **Stream** anything a person reads. Streaming does not make the call faster, but the reader
   starts at the time to first token instead of the time to last token.
2. **Shorten outputs** before you shop for a faster model. Asking for a terse format often halves
   latency and output cost at the same time.
3. **Parallelise independent calls.** Three sequential calls of 2 seconds each is 6 seconds; in
   parallel it is 2.

## Throughput and concurrency

Little's law connects arrival rate, duration and concurrency:

$$
\text{concurrent requests} = \text{arrival rate} \times \text{time per request}
$$

At 20 requests per second and 6 seconds per request, 120 requests are in flight at any moment. That
number sizes connection pools, websocket servers, rate-limit tiers and, if you self-host, GPU
memory. API providers limit requests per minute and tokens per minute (input and output
separately); check that the peak, not the average, fits inside your tier.

Daily traffic is not flat. For business tools, assume 80% of the day's requests arrive in about 8
hours, and a peak hour at about twice the average of those hours. For consumer apps, check the
evening peak. Size for the peak; pay for the average only if your capacity is elastic.

## Memory on a GPU

You need this only if you self-host (see [System 39](../systems/39-self-hosted-inference.qmd)), but
when you do, it decides everything.

**Weights.** Parameters times bytes per parameter. A 70B-parameter model such as Llama 3.3 70B
needs about {{< var f.f2.w70_fp16 >}} GB in 16-bit precision, {{< var f.f2.w70_fp8 >}} GB in FP8 and
{{< var f.f2.w70_int4 >}} GB in 4-bit. An H100 has 80 GB.

**KV cache.** Every token in every active sequence stores a key and a value vector in every layer:

$$
\text{KV bytes per token} = 2 \times \text{layers} \times \text{KV heads} \times \text{head dim} \times \text{bytes}
$$

For Llama 3.3 70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, FP16) that is
{{< var f.f2.kv70_kb >}} KB per token, so one 8,192-token sequence holds
{{< var f.f2.kv70_8k_gb >}} GB. For Llama 3.1 8B it is {{< var f.f2.kv8_kb >}} KB per token.
Whatever memory is left after the weights decides how many sequences you can serve at once, which
decides throughput.

**Decode is memory-bound.** Producing one token for one sequence means reading every weight once.
An H100 reads {{< var f.f2.h100_bw >}} TB/s, so a 70B model in FP8 split across two H100s cannot
produce more than about {{< var f.f2.decode_ceiling_70_fp8_tp2 >}} tokens per second for a single
stream, however fast the arithmetic units are. Batching is how self-hosting becomes economical:
one read of the weights serves every sequence in the batch, so 64 sequences cost barely more per
step than one.

**Prefill is compute-bound.** Processing the prompt costs about $2 \times \text{parameters}$
floating-point operations per token. At a realistic 40% of the H100's FP8 peak, a 70B model
prefills about {{< var f.f2.prefill_tok_s >}} tokens per second per GPU.

## Storage for retrieval

$$
\text{index bytes} \approx \text{chunks} \times \text{dimensions} \times 4 \times 1.5
$$

Four bytes per float32 dimension, and about 1.5 times overhead for an HNSW graph index. A million
chunks of 1,024 dimensions is about 6 GB. Most corpora are smaller than people expect: 40,000 wiki
pages make about 180,000 chunks, under 2 GB with 1,536-dimension vectors. Storage is rarely the
constraint. Re-embedding the corpus when you change embedding models is the cost to plan for.

## Constants worth memorising

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Words per English token | about 0.75 |
| Output price / input price | 4x to 8x; 5x on current Claude and GPT models |
| Hosted time to first token | 300 ms to 1.5 s |
| Hosted decode speed | 40 to 150 tokens/s per stream |
| Frontier / small model price ratio | about {{< var f.ratio.frontier_small >}}x |
| Batch API discount | 50% |
| Prompt cache read | 2.5% to 10% of the input price, depending on the model |
| H100 memory and bandwidth | 80 GB, {{< var f.f2.h100_bw >}} TB/s |
| 8x H100 on AWS (p5.48xlarge, on-demand) | {{< var f.f2.p5_hour >}}/hour, about {{< var f.f2.p5_month >}}/month |
| Hours in a month | 730 |
